principles: Keep the four life-cycle stages explicit and sequential.
Use monarch-specific facts because one monarch and milkweed sequence is visually locked across the book.
Replace dramatic simplifications with concrete biological actions.

pages.reason: Uses the standard two-word spelling life cycle and keeps the four-stage overview concise.
pages.text: A butterfly's life has four stages. This is called a life cycle. Each stage looks very different from the one before.

pages.reason: Corrects the suggestion that the caterpillar eats the leaf while still inside its egg and locks the host plant.
pages.text: Stage one: a monarch butterfly lays a tiny egg on a milkweed leaf. The egg is no bigger than a pinhead. After it hatches, the leaf will be food for the caterpillar.

pages.reason: Removes the personified only-job claim and adds the important growth action of shedding skin.
pages.text: Stage two: the egg hatches into a caterpillar. It eats milkweed and grows quickly. It sheds its skin several times. A new caterpillar may eat its own eggshell first.

pages.reason: Corrects the false implication that a monarch spins a hard shell around itself.
pages.text: Stage three: the caterpillar hangs upside down. It sheds its skin one last time, revealing a green chrysalis. Inside, a great change begins.

pages.reason: Replaces the misleading claim that the caterpillar breaks down completely and qualifies the development time.
pages.text: Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar's body changes into a butterfly. This process is called metamorphosis. For a monarch, it often takes about two weeks.

pages.reason: Explains how newly emerged wings expand, dry, and harden more accurately.
pages.text: Stage four: the butterfly pushes out of the chrysalis. It hangs still and pumps fluid into its soft, crumpled wings. The wings spread out, dry, and harden.

pages.reason: Connects nectar feeding to the proboscis and describes foot taste sensors without implying that nectar is eaten.
pages.text: Butterflies drink nectar through a long tube called a proboscis. They use their eyes and antennae to find flowers. They also taste plants with sensors on their feet.

pages.reason: Distinguishes the one-generation southward flight from the multi-generation return north.
pages.text: In autumn, some monarchs fly thousands of kilometres south to Mexico. They rest for winter in mountain forests. In spring, several new generations make the journey north.
